Q: What limitations do closures have in Python compared to language X closures? A:

Fixed in Python 3 via the nonlocal statement:

The nonlocal statement causes the listed identifiers to refer to previously bound variables in the nearest enclosing scope excluding globals. This is important because the default behavior for binding is to search the local namespace first. The statement allows encapsulated code to rebind variables outside of the local scope besides the global (module) scope.

Q: How can I see the amount of changes (additions, deletions) in a GitHub pull request, excluding package-lock.json? A:

If your primary branch is called main then git diff main..HEAD --stat -- . ":(exclude)package-lock.json"

This selects a range of changes (with ..) between main and the current commit, HEAD, and only shows the file stats. The heavy lifting is that bit at the end which is a git patchspec to hide any changes to that file.

Q: How can I write bytes to a file in Python 3 without knowing the encoding? A:

Specify binary mode, 'b', when you open your file:

with open('myfile.txt', 'wb') as w:
    w.write(bytes)

https://docs.python.org/3.3/library/functions.html#open

Q: How to select elements from list in random order A:

In Postgres 16 and higher, there's array_shuffle(): demo at db<>fiddle

select unnest(array_shuffle(array['I','Q','C','K','X','T','S','NE']));
unnest
S
I
NE
C
T
K
Q
X

As it says on the tin, each time you run it, it shuffles the array pseudo-randomly. Unlike random(), it does not rely on the session-wide seed you can control with setseed(), so there's no risk something else will accidentally affect its randomness by tweaking the shared seed.

Also, it avoids constant folding you experienced in your test:

update test
set test=array_to_string(array_shuffle(ARRAY['I','Q','C','K','X','T','S','NE']),',')
returning test;
test
T,Q,I,NE,C,X,S,K
C,S,NE,K,I,T,X,Q

To get a subset of those elements that you'd get from adding a limit clause in your original approach, you can use array_sample(), or a slice:

select array_sample(array['I','Q','C','K','X','T','S','NE'],4);

select (array_shuffle(array['I','Q','C','K','X','T','S','NE']))[:4];

Q: Create a custom cast (that also accepts $null) A:

tl;dr

  • You can only achieve what you want via a constructor, not also with a cast.

  • Thus, your only options are:

    # Method syntax
[Checkbox]::new($null).ToString()

# New-Object alternative (more awkward)
(New-Object Checkbox @($null)).ToString()

Casts in PowerShell do double duty in PowerShell:

  • Type conversion, similar to C#, for instance, but with much more flexibility. This includes both true conversions from one type to another (e.g. [int] 1.1) as well as casting to a specific interface a type implements in the context of .NET method overload resolution (e.g. [System.Collections.IDictionary] @{ foo=42 }; see also below).

  • Instance construction: unlike in C#, cast syntax can situationally construct instances of the specified type, depending on the available constructors and the cast argument.

However, type-conversion casts take precedence and [Checkbox] $null is a valid "conversion": since your custom [Checkbox] type is (invariably) a .NET reference type, $null can be cast to it,[1] and the result of this expression is simply $null.

As for the usefulness of such casts: Given that $null has no inherent type, something like [Checkbox] $null can guide overload resolution in .NET method calls, i.e. to unambiguously call the intended overload among multiple ones.

To give a quick example:

Here's a sample class with a static ::Bar() method that has two overloads that differ only in the type of their one and only parameter; both types are .NET reference types and may therefore be $null:

class Foo {
  static [string] Bar([regex] $regex) { return "[regex] overload" }
  static [string] Bar([hashtable] $hashtable) { return "[hashtable] overload" }
}

Now try to call one of the overloads of the static ::Bar() method with $null as the argument: To unambiguously select the desired overload you must use a cast:

# ERROR due to ambiguity:
# 'Multiple ambiguous overloads found for "Bar" and the argument count: "1".'
[Foo]::Bar($null)

# OK: Cast needed to select the desired overload.
# -> "[regex] overload"
[Foo]::Bar([regex] $null)

[1] PowerShell also allows casting $null to select value types, namely .NET's primitive types, such as [int], [double], ... However, this does not translate to a constructor call (said types do not have constructors with parameters); rather, these are built-in, PowerShell-specific conversions that interpret $null as (type-appropriate) 0; e.g., [int] $null yields as 0 (as an [int]).
Note that this is not supported for non-primitive value types; e.g., [datetime] $null yields an error.

Q: Dealing with brackets in email subject line A:

Query should be like
sFilter = "[CompanyName] = 'Microsoft'"
or
sFilter = "[CompanyName] = ""Microsoft"""
"brackets" should not interfere with the search in any way.
Try
Query = "[Subject] = " &"'" & subject & "'"

See doc

Q: How to convert a UTC datetime to a local datetime using only standard library? A:

In Python 3.3+:

from datetime import datetime, timezone

def utc_to_local(utc_dt):
    return utc_dt.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).astimezone(tz=None)

In Python 2/3:

import calendar
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def utc_to_local(utc_dt):
    # get integer timestamp to avoid precision lost
    timestamp = calendar.timegm(utc_dt.timetuple())
    local_dt = datetime.fromtimestamp(timestamp)
    assert utc_dt.resolution >= timedelta(microseconds=1)
    return local_dt.replace(microsecond=utc_dt.microsecond)

Using pytz (both Python 2/3):

import pytz

local_tz = pytz.timezone('Europe/Moscow') # use your local timezone name here
# NOTE: pytz.reference.LocalTimezone() would produce wrong result here

## You could use `tzlocal` module to get local timezone on Unix and Win32
# from tzlocal import get_localzone # $ pip install tzlocal

# # get local timezone
# local_tz = get_localzone()

def utc_to_local(utc_dt):
    local_dt = utc_dt.replace(tzinfo=pytz.utc).astimezone(local_tz)
    return local_tz.normalize(local_dt) # .normalize might be unnecessary

Example

def aslocaltimestr(utc_dt):
    return utc_to_local(utc_dt).strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%f %Z%z')

print(aslocaltimestr(datetime(2010,  6, 6, 17, 29, 7, 730000)))
print(aslocaltimestr(datetime(2010, 12, 6, 17, 29, 7, 730000)))
print(aslocaltimestr(datetime.utcnow()))

Output

Python 3.3

2010-06-06 21:29:07.730000 MSD+0400
2010-12-06 20:29:07.730000 MSK+0300
2012-11-08 14:19:50.093745 MSK+0400

Python 2

2010-06-06 21:29:07.730000
2010-12-06 20:29:07.730000
2012-11-08 14:19:50.093911

pytz

2010-06-06 21:29:07.730000 MSD+0400
2010-12-06 20:29:07.730000 MSK+0300
2012-11-08 14:19:50.146917 MSK+0400

Note: it takes into account DST and the recent change of utc offset for MSK timezone.

I don't know whether non-pytz solutions work on Windows.

Q: Uncaught Invariant Violation: Rendered more hooks than during the previous render A:

I just moved upwards one hook initialization

const match = useMatch('/items/:id')

in the component and the error disappeared.
